What changes when the regime applies?

The way the conflict is narrated changes, because attention moves from the isolated event to the supply program. The way it is proved changes, because opacity becomes part of the legal problem. And the way it is remedied changes, because the response is no longer automatically satisfied with money when the harm reaches continuity, intelligibility, functional position, practical trust or permanence.

In each family the harmful mechanism, the evidentiary problem and the required restoration are kept distinct. This does not mean the regime works for almost everything. The three dimensions are seen in connection, but they are not confused.
Harmful modulation is not to be confused with its proof. The evidentiary difficulty is not to be confused with the harm itself.<1>p. 788</1>
What emerges from the analysis of the models is not, therefore, the conclusion that the IOC would serve for almost everything.<1>p. 788</1>

And the way of remedying changes, because the response can no longer be automatically satisfied with pecuniary equivalents whenever the harm reaches continuity, intelligibility, functional position, practical trust or conditions of permanence in enjoyment.<1>p. 788</1>

By keeping distinguishable, in each platform family, the mechanism of harmful modulation, the corresponding evidentiary problem and the rationale of restoration required by the regime, both empty abstraction and casuistic dispersion are avoided.<1>p. 788</1>
Do these pages accuse any company?

Showing the mechanism is not condemning the service. Not every platform reproduces the same problem, and those that do don't do it with the same force. Nor does every technology-mediated relationship fall under consumer protection.
What these pages do is test whether the same questions remain useful when the environment changes. They don't say that a given company is abusive. They say where to look.

The point, here, is not to gather digital examples under a single heading by mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment<1>p. 755</1>
Not every economically technology-mediated relationship will justify the application of the CDC.<1>p. 780</1>
The laboratory of origin
The typology was developed in a laboratory of origin, with a scope of illustrative application. The sections below develop it in the full text.

On the plane of illustrative application, the work takes as its privileged <1>locus</1> the ecosystem of products and services of the multinational <2>Riot Games</2>, focusing on the game <3>League of </3> <4>p. 37</4> <5>Legends</5> and its extensions on associated platforms. This scope does not intend to exhaust the diversity of the global interactive entertainment industry, but to offer a field of exemplification in which typical structures of semiotic governance, practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, monetization models based on digital goods and recurring patterns of friction between consumers and supplier become particularly clear.<6>p. 36-37</6>

<1>Who decides what you see in an online store?</1><2>Infrastructure and intermediation IOCs</2>

Online stores, social networks and ad platforms usually say they only bring the parties together, like a neutral town square. In practice, they choose what appears first, what stays hidden, who looks trustworthy, what is comparable and what takes a while to arrive.

In other words, whoever buys or sells doesn't see the market. They see the market through the platform's filters. Rankings, reputation, featured spots and recommendations are not details of the shop window, because they are part of what it delivers and they weigh on expectation, on perceived risk and on choice.
A shop window seen through several stacked lenses, each one hiding or enlarging a part of what is for sale.
How do you prove what the shop window hid?

It isn't enough to look at the product that arrived or the post that vanished. You need to rebuild the whole shop window, with the order of the offers, what was a paid ad and what wasn't, the reviews, the trust badges and the reach of each thing.

The most common mistake is to treat the screen as mere decoration. It is part of what the platform supplies, and the way it highlights and hides weighs on your whole choice, and not only on the purchase that went wrong at the end.
It is not enough to examine the final product acquired or the individual content removed, prioritized or hidden. It is necessary to reconstruct the architecture of the experience.<1>p. 763</1>
This includes, depending on the case, the form of presentation of the offers, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of reviews and reputations [...]<1>p. 763</1>
The first is the tendency to treat the interface as mere visual support, and not as a constitutive part of the supply.<1>p. 763</1>
What can you ask of whoever organizes the shop window?

The path is to demand duties over the very way things are organized. It is fair to ask whether it was clear what was sponsored, whether the reputation shown could be checked and whether the lack of clarity in the criteria got in the way of comparing the offers.
When the same company referees the shop window and also profits from what happens in it, the issue may even reach competition among sellers.
The possible dogmatic consequence, in this environment, tends to gravitate around procedural duties of controllability of interface governance.<1>p. 764</1>

It becomes necessary to examine, in an IOC key, whether there was adequate information about the nature of the intermediation, whether the distinction between organic priority and sponsored priority was materially intelligible, whether the reputation displayed was functionally verifiable [...]<1>p. 764</1>

In more serious hypotheses, especially when the platform acts simultaneously as arbiter of the environment and as an economic agent interested in its results, the opacity of the ranking may also dialogue with broader abusive practices and with competition repercussions of their own.<1>p. 764</1>
Why is intermediation not neutral?

The utility is not exhausted in the good, the content or the advertiser at the end of the chain. It is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics. The platform selects, ranks, highlights, hides and reorganizes the way the environment becomes perceptible. Rankings, reputation, featured placement, recommendation and reach modulation are part of the functional utility. On marketplaces, the consumer chooses within a field already pre-interpreted. On social networks, the same mechanism reappears, because the platform manages the way content enters the field of perception.
The platform, therefore, produces the perceptible market itself.<1>p. 762</1>
What is offered, in legally relevant terms, is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics<1>p. 761</1>
They select, rank, highlight, hide, bring closer, delay, prioritize and reorganize the way in which the reality of the environment becomes perceptible to the user.<1>p. 761</1>
Rankings, reputation, featured placement, recommendation, prioritization and reach modulation are not peripheral elements.<1>p. 761</1>
He chooses within a field already pre-interpreted by the platform.<1>p. 762</1>
It manages the way in which these contents enter the user's field of perception and how their relevance is socially stabilized.<1>p. 762</1>
What vulnerability does the interface produce?

The asymmetry is not only one of quantity of information. It is one of constitution of the relevant field of the decision. The platform defines what stands out, what is hidden, what seems more trustworthy and what becomes almost invisible. The promise also lies in the implicit intelligibility of the market or of social circulation, and it is affected when governed by opaque or non-auditable criteria.
He faces an asymmetry of constitution of the relevant field of the decision.<1>p. 763</1>

The platform defines what stands out, what is hidden, what seems more trustworthy, what acquires the appearance of consensus, what emerges as comparable and what becomes practically invisible.<1>p. 763</1>
It also lies in the implicit promise of intelligibility of the market or of social circulation.<1>p. 763</1>
How is the experience reconstructed?

It is not enough to examine the final product or the removed content. It is necessary to reconstruct the presentation of the offers, the distinction between organic and paid results, reviews and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the signals of trustworthiness and the moderation criteria. On social networks, the feed, the recommendation and the reach. On marketplaces, ranking, featured placement, seller rating and sponsorship. Who is in charge of work done through an app? · Platforms · Lex Plataformae
<1>Who is in charge of work done through an app?</1><2>Productivity IOCs under the gig economy</2>

For people who work this way, the app supplies more than a payment per task. It supplies the very environment in which the work becomes possible, and that environment is governed by it. That is why it isn't enough to look at what the contract says about autonomy. You have to look at who actually organizes access to demand, the possible pay and staying in the flow.
A city map in which the route of a delivery bicycle is drawn by an enormous hand, with rating stars floating over the path.
How do you prove the app's rule changed?

Showing that earnings fell or that the account was blocked once isn't enough. You need to link the loss to the way the app governs the work, with the history of requests, the variations in pay, the alerts, the criteria disclosed or hidden and the records of restriction.
And a drop in earnings isn't always a natural risk of the activity. It may come from a rule change that nobody explained.

It is not enough to demonstrate that there was a reduction in earnings or an isolated block. It is necessary to reconstruct the relationship between the governance mechanism and the functional impact.<1>p. 768</1>

This may involve history of requests, variations in remuneration, internal communications of the app, performance alerts, criteria disclosed or omitted, records of restriction, rating patterns and comparative data on the change in the environment.<1>p. 768</1>
The first is treating the fluctuation of earnings as a pure natural risk of the activity, when it may result from an opaque unilateral reconfiguration of the distribution infrastructure.<1>p. 768</1>
What can you ask for when the app changes the rule?
An active account doesn't prove nothing changed. The question is whether your place in the app remains equivalent to the one that sustained your expectation of earnings and of staying on.

When the change empties that place, it may be possible to demand the records, the reasons for the restrictions, the review of the criteria and the restoration of what was degraded. This doesn't turn everything into a labor matter, but it also doesn't let the contract that speaks of autonomy end the conversation.

The legal test cannot be only whether the account remains active. It needs to be whether the partner's functional position in the environment remains substantially equivalent to the one that structured his legitimate expectation of earnings and permanence.<1>p. 767-768</1>

The most adequate institutional response will tend to favor preservation and display of minimum records, duties of verifiable reasoning, review of restriction criteria, intelligibility about relevant parameters of distribution of opportunities and functional restoration of the regime [...]<1>p. 768</1>
[...] does not dissolve the subtype into undifferentiated labor law, but neither does it let itself be neutralized by contractual self-descriptions of formal autonomy.<1>p. 768</1>
What does the platform supply to those who work on it?

A private infrastructure of economic possibility. It organizes access to demand, distribution of requests, predictability of pay, permanence in the productive flow, reputational criteria, prioritization and sanction. The self-description as intermediary and the formal freedom to switch the app on and off do not solve the problem. The examination falls on the supply regime, without automatically reclassifying the relationship under the categories of the employment contract and without reducing it to the dichotomy between autonomy and subordination.
The platform asserts independence at the contractual end and intensifies governance at the operational end.<1>p. 767</1>
The legally relevant question is not only whether the platform describes itself as an intermediary or whether the partner is formally free to switch the app on and off.<1>p. 766</1>

The central point lies not only in asserting algorithmic subordination in the abstract, nor in automatically reclassifying the whole relationship under traditional categories of the employment contract.<1>p. 766</1>
That is why the dogmatic problem cannot be reduced to the simplistic dichotomy between autonomy and subordination.<1>p. 767</1>
What vulnerability does productive dependence add?

Metrics, incentive messages, quality alerts, promotions, acceptance patterns, pricing dynamics and performance notifications work as a private language for governing conduct. The partner depends on these signs to know his own position, the expectation of earnings and the risk of restriction or exclusion. The opacity falls on the material living conditions of those who depend on the environment to work.

When is the harm collective?

It is not enough that many consumers are hit by similar facts. Collective redress is justified when the harmful source is unitary, repeatable and built into the ordinary functioning of the platform. Repeated opacity, persistent absence of history and non-auditable mutability form a defect of regime. This is architecture harm, produced by the design of the supply. The effects are not homogeneous, but the matrix is common.
The harm, thus, is not only to the individual result of consumption. It is to the institutional verifiability of the supply.<1>p. 774</1>
The basis of collective redress, here, does not lie only in the circumstance that many consumers may be hit by similar facts.<1>p. 774</1>
Collective redress is justified when the harmful source remains unitary, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary functioning of the platform.<1>p. 774</1>
Repeated opacity, persistent absence of history and non-auditable mutability form, together, a defect of regime.<1>p. 774</1>
The impact is not homogeneous in all its effects, but it is common in its matrix.<1>p. 776</1>
What can collective redress impose?

Inhibitory, procedural and analytical measures that reintroduce verifiability, such as preservation of minimum records, verifiable reasoning for relevant sanctions, accessible history of changes and minimum operational criteria for distribution, priority or ranking. Individual protection remains indispensable to repair concrete losses. Treatment that is only atomized tends to monetize episodes without changing the structure and to turn the systemic difficulty of proof into a private failure of dispersed consumers.
Collective redress thus proves particularly suited to imposing inhibitory, procedural and analytical measures capable of reintroducing institutional verifiability into the environment.<1>p. 775</1>

This may involve duties of preservation of minimum records, a requirement of verifiable reasoning for materially relevant sanctions, maintenance of an accessible history of relevant changes, explicit statement of minimum operational criteria of distribution, priority or ranking<1>p. 775</1>
This does not mean abolishing the role of individual protection.<1>p. 775</1>
On the one hand, it monetizes episodes without changing the machine that reproduces them.<1>p. 776</1>

Open auditability · The jurist's way · Lex Plataformae
<1>The jurist's way</1>
Open auditability

Open auditability is the minimum threshold of external verifiability that makes it possible to reconstruct what the supplier changed, when, why and with what effect, whenever the change or the sanction significantly affects the enjoyment of an Immaterial Object of Consumption. The requirement arises within the CDC, has a delimited scope and does not yield to secrecy or to technical complexity.
What problem does open auditability solve?

In a continuous digital service, asking whether the platform may change the environment leads to little, because changing is part of the way the service is rendered. The legal problem is to distinguish legitimate mutation from the mutation that breaks the balance of the supply, degrades the promised enjoyment or makes the very possibility of control opaque. This last hypothesis has a trait of its own, since a good part of the disputes do not arise from abrupt suppression, but from progressive changes, interface changes and visibility adjustments that seem trivial when taken one by one. The consumer keeps the account, keeps seeing the object and keeps accessing the platform, while the utility may fall and, with it, the consumer's capacity to prove the fall.
In IOCs, mutability exists, but it does not hover above the Law.<1>p. 635</1>

The legal problem, therefore, lies not in finding out whether the platform may alter the environment, but in establishing the criteria by which legitimate mutation is distinguished from the mutation that breaks the balance of the supply, degrades the promised enjoyment or makes opaque the very possibility of control.<1>p. 635</1>

The consumer remains formally “inside” the ecosystem, keeps the account, keeps seeing the object, can keep accessing the platform. Even so, the utility enjoyed may be substantially lowered, and the capacity to prove this lowering may be simultaneously eroded by the very way the environment is administered.<1>p. 635</1>

The difficulty lies in who keeps the information. The supplier controls the architecture, the criteria for change, the logs, which are the automatic records of what the system did, the moment of the change and the very means by which it will be perceived. With this, it concentrates the power to reconfigure and also the power to narrate alone what happened. The effect appears in two images, that of the supplier who comes to hold the practical monopoly of the real and that of the consumer reduced to a bearer of symptoms, who feels having lost something important, but cannot demonstrate what was lost, how it was lost or why the loss goes beyond the trivial annoyance of networked life.
The supplier comes to hold the practical monopoly of the “real”, and the consumer is reduced to a bearer of symptoms, without a common language that allows comparison and control.<1>p. 473</1>

That is why opacity, in these environments, is not only a technical feature, and it works as an asymmetric distribution of power within the relationship. Whoever controls the criteria, the records, the memory of the system and the language in which events can be described also concentrates the capacity to define what will be considered demonstrable. Without a verifiable minimum, the conflict tends to become an unequal confrontation between the consumer's subjective experience and a self-justifying business version, and private governance also becomes power over the institutional conditions of proof. It is against this practical immunity that the parameter is directed.

Whoever controls the criteria for change, the records of what was done, the memory of the system and the language in which these events can be described also concentrates the capacity to define what will be considered demonstrable.<1>p. 728</1>
Without minimum auditability, the conflict tends to be degraded into an unequal confrontation between the consumer's subjective experience and a formally self-justified business version.<1>p. 728</1>
Private governance then ceases to be only a power to modulate enjoyment and also becomes a power to control the institutional conditions of proof.<1>p. 728</1>
Why do neither total transparency nor published information solve it?

The debate usually gets stuck between two positions. One holds that any transparency requirement compromises trade secrets, innovation or business autonomy, and the other imagines that there is only effective control with complete opening of the internal functioning. Both fail, and the clash is a binary theater, because the first turns technical complexity into an alibi and the second confuses legal protection with invasion of the productive environment. The refusal has a practical effect, since conditioning control on total transparency produces paralysis, and accepting mutability as a neutral given normalizes substantial degradations as mere operational variation.

On one side, it is argued that any transparency requirement would compromise trade secrets, innovation or business autonomy. On the other, it is imagined that control would only be effective if there were complete opening of the platform's internal functioning. Both positions are bad. The first turns technical complexity into an alibi for irresponsibility. The second confuses legal protection with total invasion of the productive environment. Open auditability rejects this binary theater.<1>p. 727</1>
The attempt to condition the legal control of opaque ecosystems on total transparency misses the target and produces paralysis.<1>p. 481</1>

The frustration of the enjoyment bundle then tends to present itself as noise, and the legal response oscillates between two equally unproductive extremes: requiring total transparency incompatible with the functioning of the technical-organizational environment or accepting mutability as a neutral given, normalizing substantial degradations as mere operational variation.<1>p. 469</1>

The supplier's usual answer is that the information is already available, in the terms, in the cross-references, in the frequently asked questions and in the update history. This is not enough, because information, under the CDC, does not fulfill its function merely by existing somewhere. What matters is its reconstructive and decisional usefulness, that is, serving to know what occurred and to decide what to do. When this is missing, there is documentary staging and performative transparency, in which the consumer knows that something changed, but cannot discern what changed, by what criterion, with what practical effect and how to demonstrate the impact.
The change exists, the notice exists, the document exists, the history exists, but the useful reconstruction of the event does not exist.<1>p. 641</1>

Information, under the CDC, does not fulfill its function merely because it exists somewhere, nor because it was deposited in lengthy documents, cross-references, FAQs or update histories that the consumer will hardly locate, understand and connect to the actual impact suffered. What matters is its reconstructive and decisional usefulness.<1>p. 641</1>
Instead of real transparency, there is only a documentary staging of compliance, a situation incompatible with the standard of adequate and conspicuous information required by the CDC<1>p. 640</1>

The contemporary problem, therefore, is not only the absence of information, but its strategic organization. The platform may flood the consumer with announcements, changelogs, which are the public records of changes, on-screen notices, policies and frequently asked questions, and still preserve the effective monopoly over the intelligibility of what matters. Added to the technical concentration of records, this mutability produces a private evidentiary fortress.
This effect is all the more important because the contemporary problem is not only absence of information, but strategic organization of information.<1>p. 646</1>

The platform may flood the consumer with announcements, changelogs, banners, dialog boxes, policies, disclaimers and FAQs, and still preserve for itself the effective monopoly over the intelligibility of what matters.<1>p. 646</1>
Without this, the mutability of the service and the technical concentration of records produce, together, a kind of private evidentiary fortress.<1>p. 646</1>

Nor do the two customary dogmatic exits help. The civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good is narrow for governed consumption, and the microscopic analysis of isolated clauses starts from the assumption that the platform only produces unlawfulness through badly drafted contractual sentences. The focus comes to fall on the architecture of the supply and on the material controllability of its mutations.

In governed ecosystems, the relevant unlawful act often lies not in a heroically villainous clause, but in the way the environment changes, justifies itself poorly, erases traces and preserves only the formal appearance of continuity.<1>p. 639</1>

It is no longer necessary to reduce the conflict to a civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good, which would be narrow for governed consumption. Nor is there a need to remain tied to the microscopic analysis of isolated clauses, as if the platform only produced unlawfulness through badly drafted contractual sentences. The focus comes to fall on the architecture of the supply and on the material controllability of its mutations.<1>p. 639</1>
Is open auditability a new right?

No, and precision matters for whoever will ground a claim. Open auditability is neither an autonomous positive right nor an institute foreign to the consumer microsystem. It is an internal development of three things the system already has, the duty to inform, objective good faith and the facilitation of the consumer's defense. Called sometimes an operator, sometimes a standard, sometimes a parameter, it designates in every case a standard of requirement that the interpreter applies to the case, of technically qualified transparency usable by institutions. It is enforceable whenever the supplier makes relevant changes, sanctions or reconfigurations capable of reaching the core of enjoyment.

A standard of minimum verifiability, compatible with the protection of software and of business secrecy, but incompatible with the opaque shielding of execution; a development of the duty to inform, of objective good faith and of the facilitation of the consumer's defense; a criterion for reducing evidentiary and informational asymmetry; and an institutional condition for relevant mutations of the IOC to cease being accepted as accomplished facts narrated only by the supplier itself.<1>p. 648</1>

Open auditability designates, in continuous digital services, a standard of technically qualified and institutionally usable transparency, enforceable whenever the supplier makes relevant changes, sanctions or reconfigurations capable of reaching the core of enjoyment of the Immaterial Object of Consumption.<1>p. 639-640</1>

The first support is the duty to inform. The manual by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa requires correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information, records the need for prior control of the contract by the consumer and recalls that information is part of the contractual content and, if it fails, may represent a quality defect. Ricardo Morishita Wada adds that leaving the time for performance under the supplier's exclusive definition takes away the consumer's capacity for control, and Bruno Miragem treats the duty to inform as a duty of clarification, whose fulfillment the supplier itself has the burden of demonstrating and whose breach may attract Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. On this basis the step that grounds the category is taken. Whoever alters central elements of enjoyment without giving an intelligible basis for reconstructing what occurred does not merely communicate poorly, because that supplier prevents control and worsens the consumer's position in the relationship.
The Manual synthesizes this standard by requiring “correct”, “clear”, “precise” and “conspicuous” information <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 128])</2>.<3>p. 640</3>

In addition, clear and adequate information governs the pre-contractual moment, the conclusion of the contract, the contract itself and the post-contractual moment, affecting “the essence of the deal”, since it is part of the contractual content and, if it fails, may represent a defect in the quality of the product or service offered <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 126])</2>.<3>p. 640</3>

Not informing the time for performance, or leaving its definition to a later moment under the supplier's exclusive control, places the consumer in a situation of extreme vulnerability, because without an intelligible reconstruction of the way the obligation is performed the consumer loses capacity for control and the supplier comes to dictate unilaterally the rules of the game <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 208)</2>.<3>p. 641</3>

Adequate information about the relevant elements of the performance serves as a criterion for assessing the regular exercise of the supplier's contractual freedom; its breach may reveal abusiveness, compromise the quality of consent and even attract Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. Demonstrating that this duty was effectively fulfilled is an evidentiary burden of the supplier itself <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 412)</4>.<5>p. 643</5>

If the supplier alters obligations, usage parameters, compatibility conditions or central elements of enjoyment without providing a minimally intelligible basis for reconstructing what occurred, it does not merely communicate poorly. It prevents control.<1>p. 641</1>

The second support is objective good faith during performance. In a digital service, the performance is not exhausted in an initial delivery, because the relationship extends through updates, fixes, rebalances and sanctions, and treating this period as a neutral space would be far too crude. Claudia Lima Marques rejects the idea that there is an empty space between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the performance and describes the relationship as a continuous whole, with ancillary duties to inform, to cooperate and of loyalty. Breaching them, for the author, means nonperformance, even if partial. The long-term contract, in turn, rests more on trust and on the maintenance of quality, so that the supplier cannot reserve for itself all the intelligibility of the process of change and leave the consumer only with the imposed result.

Objective good faith, in relationships of this nature, projects continuous duties of information, cooperation, loyalty and protection of trust, so that the supplier cannot reserve for itself all the intelligibility of the process of mutation of the service and leave the consumer only with the final result already imposed<1>p. 640</1>

Breaching the duty of cooperation and loyalty means nonperformance, even if partial, including when the supplier hinders the consumer's access to his rights <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 236)</2>.<3>p. 641</3>

In relationships of continued performance, the consumer places trust not only in an initial utility, but in the minimally intelligible permanence of the relationship and in the possibility of understanding its relevant changes.<1>p. 645</1>

The third support is the facilitation of defense. Article 6, item VIII, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, according to the manual by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa, is not merely procedural in nature, because it is aimed at effective protection and at reparation, and the spirit of the Code is not to impose on the vulnerable party the proof of elements that are part of the supplier's professional risk. Since the platform concentrates records, histories, enforcement criteria and versions, the facilitation of defense and the redistribution of the burden cease to be occasional instruments and become a condition of minimum effectiveness of the regime. Open auditability then works as a technique for reducing informational and evidentiary asymmetry, which puts the conflict back on reconstructible ground.

The Manual is clear in observing that the right provided for in art. 6, VIII, although it aims to facilitate the consumer's procedural defense, is not merely procedural in nature: it is a substantive right aimed at the effective protection and reparation of the damages suffered <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 146])</2>.<3>p. 642</3>

The facilitation of defense and the redistribution of the burden of proof cease to be occasional instruments and become a condition of minimum effectiveness of the protective regime itself.<1>p. 642</1>
Open auditability, at this point, works as a technique for reducing informational and evidentiary asymmetry.<1>p. 642</1>

The systematic consequence is that the lack of auditability does not open an autonomous path of imputation. Quality defect, abusive practice and abusive clause remain the three entry doors into the CDC, the subject of the chapter on the unlawful act of architecture. The absence of auditability does not create a fourth door, but reinforces any of them, because opacity may intensify the imputation for abusive practice, aggravate the reading of the clause that shields arbitrariness and weaken the defense that there was a mere legitimate adaptation. It is a legal technology of controllability, and what it allows is to discuss defect, inadequacy, abusiveness and breach of the duty to inform on a reconstructible basis.
The same hypothesis may simultaneously reveal a quality defect, an abusive practice and an abusive clause, and in borderline cases even approach the logic of the safety defect.<1>p. 678</1>
The absence of auditability does not create an autonomous fourth door, but structurally reinforces any of the others.<1>p. 678</1>

When the platform does not preserve minimum trails, does not offer verifiable reasoning, concentrates proof and prevents reconstruction of what it altered or of the reason why it sanctioned, this opacity intensifies the imputation for abusive practice, aggravates the reading of the predisposed clause that shields arbitrariness and weakens the defense that there would have been a mere legitimate adaptation of the performance.<1>p. 678</1>
Open auditability is a legal technology of controllability.<1>p. 645</1>

This allows defect, inadequacy, abusiveness, breach of the duty to inform and breach of trust to be discussed on a reconstructible basis, and not in a crude confrontation between corporate narrative and the consumer's subjective feeling.<1>p. 645</1>
Why can the Law control without seeing everything?

Control does not depend on full transparency, and the support comes from legal theory. Humberto Ávila proposes shifting the focus from security of meaning to security of criteria, with prior parameters to face later interpretive problems, and distinguishes security from transparency. Transparency has its core in information, while security seeks argumentative rationality and the control of arbitrariness. From there, the question ceases to be opening the black box all the way down and becomes defining controllable criteria that turn modulations, that is, the continuous changes in the conditions of the service, into legally decidable alternatives.

It is in this sense that Humberto Ávila formulates an explicit turn by arguing that one should shift the focus from security of meaning to security of criteria, in order to provide, in advance, prior and abstract parameters to face later and concrete interpretive problems <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 71)</2>.<3>p. 472</3>

The question is not to open the black box all the way down, but to define prior and controllable criteria that make it possible to turn technically opaque modulations into legally decidable alternatives, without reducing control to automatic deference to complexity.<1>p. 472</1>

Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. completes the argument through the function of dogmatics. He presents it as a technology aimed at action, which carves out what is operable in the form of a decision, and recalls that the real legal decision operates with incomplete information and has as its immediate purpose to absorb insecurity, transforming undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives. On the platform, opacity tends to push the dispute toward endlessness, because there always remains a technical behind-the-scenes capable of explaining the effect. A minimum threshold operates as a mechanism of finitude, since it organizes the debate around elements that can be discussed under adversarial proceedings.
The Law does not need to see everything in order to control.<1>p. 473</1>

In platform-governed consumption, structural opacity tends to push the dispute toward endlessness, because there always remains a technical “behind” that could explain the effect. A minimum threshold of auditability operates as a mechanism of finitude, organizing the debate around elements that are reconstructible and discussable under adversarial proceedings, without the fiction of total transparency.<1>p. 474</1>

Ferraz Jr. formulates the point in terms that serve as a rule of method: “absorption of insecurity” means that the act of deciding “transforms undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives”, without promising to eliminate the conflict, but converting it into something treatable <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312])</2>.<3>p. 481</3>

Julie E. Cohen and Eros Roberto Grau explain why this control is justified. Cohen describes dominant platforms as agents that produce a territory of their own, made of protocols, data flows and algorithms, and argues that any meaningful control of this environment depends on a baseline level of information about what such mechanisms do. Grau, discussing the formation of the rule of law from Duguit, associates the legal norm with the socially organized sanction and observes that the market establishes an order produced by it. On platforms, the sanction appears as suspension, ban, lowering of visibility and blocking of features, executed by architecture and by internal procedures. When this operates as a pattern, the demand for auditability ceases to be an aesthetic transparency agenda and becomes a minimum requirement for subjecting private coercion to rational control.

Julie E. Cohen describes this power by treating dominant platforms as agents capable of producing and controlling a kind of territory of their own, which is not physical, but is built by protocols, data flows and algorithms, and which presents itself to the user as a space demarcated and protected by guarded borders <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 235)</2>.<3>p. 474</3>

Discussing the formation of the rule of law from Duguit, Grau indicates that a social norm becomes a legal norm when the mass of consciences understands that the sanction can be “socially organized” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 73)</2>.<3>p. 476</3>
The same intuition appears when Grau observes that the market posits its legal order by establishing an order produced by it <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</2>.<3>p. 476</3>

Cohen herself formulates the need for this threshold by arguing that algorithms and protocols classify subjects, shape informational flows and authorize or deny access to network resources, so that any meaningful control of the environment depends on a baseline level of information about what these mechanisms do <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 189])</2>.<3>p. 475</3>

On platforms, the sanction materializes in suspension, ban, lowering of visibility, blocking of features, restrictions on participation and multiple forms of automated or hybrid sanction, executed by architecture and by internal procedures.<1>p. 476</1>
The demand for auditability is not an aesthetic transparency agenda, but a minimum requirement for subjecting private coercion to rational control.<1>p. 476</1>
What needs to be auditable?

The trigger is the relevant impact on enjoyment, and its delimitation is rigorous so that the parameter does not slide into maximalism. Its proper field begins when the change, the unilateral modulation, the suppression, the migration, the nerf, which is the adjustment that reduces the power or usefulness of an item, the discontinuation, the reconfiguration of a rule or of the interface, or the sanction applied to the user affects enjoyment in a relevant way. Relevance may appear in access and permanence, in the functional integrity of the object, in the promised equivalences, in the symbolic position of the object in the ecosystem or in the consumer's conditions of proof and challenge. The central point is that the change must be capable of lowering enjoyment, frustrating legitimate expectation or abusively concentrating in the supplier's hands the intelligibility of what occurred.

Its proper field begins when the change, the unilateral modulation, the suppression, the migration, the nerf, the discontinuation, the reconfiguration of a rule or of the interface, or even the sanction applied to the user, affects enjoyment in a relevant way.<1>p. 642</1>

The central point is that the change must be capable of lowering enjoyment, frustrating legitimate expectation or abusively concentrating the intelligibility of what occurred in the supplier's hands.<1>p. 642</1>

The requirement is selective and functional, because it falls on what makes the dispute decidable. It reaches relevant changes in access rules, reconfigurations with functional impact, version changes that affect utility or performance, sanctions on permanence or visibility, ordinary modulations of the environment and decision criteria with material repercussion on enjoyment. None of this can remain in a zone of non-demonstration protected by the mere claim of technicality. The mention of ordinary modulations does not dispense with the trigger, because the common trait of these hypotheses is legal interference with enjoyment, and what becomes controllable is only what interferes with it.
What must be auditable is not everything, but what matters to make the dispute decidable.<1>p. 727</1>

Relevant changes in access rules, reconfigurations with functional impact, version changes that affect utility or performance, sanctions falling on permanence or visibility, ordinary modulations of the environment and decision criteria with material repercussion on enjoyment cannot remain in a zone of non-demonstration protected by the mere claim of technicality.<1>p. 727</1>
What is required is not to strip the whole system bare, but to make controllable, to a sufficient threshold, what legally interferes with enjoyment.<1>p. 727</1>

Once the trigger is present, the minimum content is more modest than the caricature of total opening and more robust than business self-justification. It comprises an intelligible record of what was changed and of the moment of the change, a minimum technical justification, understood as the declared rationale and the stated objective, a description of the relevant impacts on enjoyment and on the parameters of the object, the preservation of verifiable trails, such as histories of relevant versions and minimum logs of events, transactions or changes, and, in enforcement cases, that is, of sanctions applied by the platform itself, minimally reconstructible criteria for the measure. Added to this is the possibility of verification by qualified third parties, including protection bodies, expert examination or judicial review.

The supplier must make available, in an institutionally useful way, an intelligible record of what was changed and of the moment of the change; a minimum technical justification, that is, the declared rationale and the stated objective for the change; a description of the relevant impacts on enjoyment and on the parameters of the IOC; preservation of verifiable trails, such as histories of relevant versions, minimum logs of events, transactions or changes; and, in enforcement cases, minimally reconstructible criteria for the sanction applied.<1>p. 643</1>

In addition, there must be a possibility of verification by qualified third parties, including by protection bodies, expert examination or judicial review, without the regime of technical secrecy being used as an absolute screen against any scrutiny<1>p. 643</1>

The same requirement appears in another formulation, as a standard of verifiable reasoning. When the platform changes access rules, reconfigures features or applies sanctions that substantially affect utility, invoking generalities is not enough, and the reasoning is described by four elements, the identification of the act and of the timing of its effects, the indication of the functional impact, the statement of operational reasons with purpose and criteria of application and the indication of means of challenge and review. The two lists do not fully coincide, and reading them together is useful to the lawyer, because the first adds the trails and the qualified third party, and the second adds the path for challenge.

This minimum threshold can be described by the identification of the act of modulation and of the timing of its effects, by the indication of the functional impact on practical dimensions of enjoyment, by the statement of operational reasons with purpose and criteria of application and by the indication of means of challenge and review.<1>p. 475-476</1>

The effect is to shift the dispute from the plane of the unspeakable narrative to the plane of a verifiable reconstruction, without turning each adjustment into litigation and without requiring an exhaustive explanation.<1>p. 476</1>

The measure of sufficiency is functional. Intelligibility must be enough to identify the relevant change, relate it to the promised enjoyment, check whether the justification is compatible with the legal regime and determine whether the sanction, the change or the modulation respected minimum standards of predictability, proportionality and contestability. The addressees are the protection bodies, the Judiciary, the experts and, to some extent, the consumers themselves, who do not need to understand the system, but need to locate what was promised, what was delivered and what was reconfigured afterward.

It is a matter of ensuring sufficient verifiable elements to locate what was promised, what was actually delivered and what was later reconfigured by acts of maintenance, curation, updating, enforcement and administration of conditions of access and use.<1>p. 473</1>
What can be gathered before asking the supplier for anything?

A discipline of reconstruction can guide the start of the lawyer's work. In the passage from the game to general parameters, the reconstruction must be verifiable through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable, among them update records, declared reasons for change, access policies and internal sanction criteria, which prevents individual experiences from being mistaken for proof. Public statements by users remain in a subsidiary position, as a symptomatic record of recurring frictions, and do not replace official documents, interface records, lawsuits or decisions.

Orientation by frictions and by sector evidence does not authorize subjectivism, because the analytical discipline derives from the prior explicit statement of the conceptual lenses and from the requirement of verifiable reconstruction through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable, among which are included update records, declared rationales for change, access policies and internal sanction criteria.<1>p. 498-499</1>

On the contrary, it reorganizes it as a commitment to criteria for selecting evidence and to a theoretical regulation of what counts as relevant observation, reducing confirmation biases and preventing individual experiences from being mistaken for proof.<1>p. 499</1>
This material is not mobilized as autonomous proof of the supplier's institutional conduct, nor as a substitute for official documents, interface records, lawsuits or decisions.<1>p. 66</1>

The material onto which the parameter projects is concrete. It consists of change communications, history of relevant versions, confirmation screens, change notices, transaction records and minimum documentation of the supply flow. In the manufacture of risk and in the permanent threat of loss, the minimum signal of proof appears in applied policies, sanction communications, absence of verifiable reasoning, decisional inconsistencies and concentration of evidentiary trails in the supplier. This shows that the absence itself has signal value, because the absence of verifiable reasoning and the concentration of the trails enter the same list as the documents that exist.

Open auditability projects onto change communications, history of relevant versions, confirmation screens, change notices, transaction records, logs sufficient to trace materially relevant interventions, minimum documentation of the supply flow and a minimally intelligible statement of the criteria invoked for relevant reconfigurations.<1>p. 636</1>

The minimum signal of proof appears in applied policies, sanction communications, absence of verifiable reasoning, decisional inconsistencies and concentration of evidentiary trails in the supplier, which directly connects this family to the problem of open auditability.<1>p. 672</1>

What is in plain sight, however, does not exhaust what the parameter asks for, and gathering this material does not transfer to the consumer the burden of reconstructing the supply. The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives communicational fragments. Auditability cannot depend on the chance that the consumer archived evidence or has the technical knowledge to produce handmade comparisons.

The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives only communicational fragments, insufficient to sustain, in a common language, the comparison between the stabilized promise and the reconfigured delivery.<1>p. 471</1>

In a regime in which the supplier can update continuously and even automatically, auditability cannot depend on the chance that the consumer archived evidence or has the technical knowledge to produce handmade comparisons.<1>p. 471</1>
What does the update of an old item show about the auditable minimum?

A technically simple example is that of the visual effects updates to old cosmetics in a Riot Games game, made under the label of modernization. A cosmetic is the item that changes the character's appearance, and its value, in an environment that depends on visual signals and social recognition, is not exhausted in being listed in the inventory. It includes the way the item presents itself in the match, the clarity with which it communicates an ability, the visual weight the user experiences and the public distinction from the common versions. When this set changes persistently, the answer that the item is still there does not settle the question, because the core of the utility may have been reconfigured.

In an environment in which enjoyment depends on visual signals, legibility and social recognition, the functional value of the cosmetic is not exhausted in its formal existence in the inventory.<1>p. 469</1>
When this set is altered persistently, equivalence is not settled with the answer that the item “is still there”, because the core of the utility enjoyed may have been reconfigured.<1>p. 470</1>

A good part of the data is public. The Terms of Service provide that the company may use background patches, which are update packages installed automatically, with or without prior notice. A public text by the company describes the program as an improvement in consistency, legibility and graphic quality and states that the goals are ranked in order of importance, so that gameplay legibility will always prevail over thematic resonance. What results is an institutional decision pattern, and not an isolated event, without contesting the legitimacy of the pursuit of clarity, which is understandable and, from the ecosystem's point of view, may be desirable.

In addition, it is provided that the company may “use background patches” to automatically update games and software “with or without prior notice” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 470</3>

In stating its criteria, the text includes ranked goals and a hierarchy of importance, arguing that one of the goals is to “reduce overall visual noise”, for example by “reducing the ‘invasion’ of textures that have many fine and unnecessary details”, and also states that the goals are “ranked in order of importance”, so that “gameplay legibility will always prevail over thematic resonance” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022a)</2>.<3>p. 470</3>

The point is not to contest the legitimacy of the pursuit of clarity, but to recognize that the application of these criteria may, in specific cases, reconfigure the core of utility that motivated the purchase of a cosmetic, especially when part of the value is tied to the visual experience, to distinction and to the “weight” perceived in game.<1>p. 470</1>

Read through the elements of the auditable minimum, the example shows that compliance may be partial. The declared reason and the criteria exist, and the Patch Notes record changes by patch, with titles and dates. This channel is useful for general information, but it was not designed as a comparative tool for those who need to reconstruct the before and after of a specific cosmetic. What is missing, from the consumption point of view, is a stable standard of comparison capable of recognizing when modernization alters what justified the price and the choice. For these cases, there are two ways out, clearer public criteria for change or restoration mechanisms as automated as the update, which dispense with impossible proof when the impact is relevant.

The official “Patch Notes” channel works as the recurring public record of changes to the game, organized in periodic entries, by patch, with titles and dates <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2>.<3>p. 471</3>

The format is useful for general information and for minimum communicational transparency, but it is not designed as a tool of comparative auditability aimed at the consumer who needs to technically reconstruct a before and after of a specific cosmetic, with objective parameters of demonstration.<1>p. 471</1>

What is missing, from the consumption point of view, is a stable standard of comparison capable of recognizing when modernization alters what justified the price and the choice, especially in items whose value depends on the visual experience and on public distinction.<1>p. 471</1>

If the system does not deliver, as a standard, sufficient comparative elements, the control of functional downgrading requires either clearer public criteria for change or equally automated restoration mechanisms that dispense with impossible proof when the impact is relevant.<1>p. 471</1>

The example needs a caution, because any merely cosmetic change falls outside the trigger, and mere aesthetic preference for an old experience is not enough. The possible reconciliation goes through the core that was sold. Changing a cosmetic item is not, for that reason alone, a cosmetic change in that sense, and the case enters the parameter when part of the acquired value is tied to the visual experience and to public distinction. Even so, auditability only prepares the decision. If the change preserves the core of utility, performance continues. If it significantly lowers what structured the utility for that consumer, the restoration must include, at least, mechanisms of choice, such as a refund, credit or exchange for an item of equivalent value, without requiring of the consumer the impossible proof of a black box.
Equivalence is not mere aesthetic preference for an old experience, nor nonconformity with ordinary variations of the service.<1>p. 477</1>

If the change preserves the core of utility, performance continues. If the change significantly lowers what structured the utility for that consumer, the restoration must include, at least, mechanisms of choice that prevent captivity by surprise, with alternatives such as refund, credit, exchange for another cosmetic of equivalent value or analogous forms of recovering the investment for the consumer's reinsertion into the ecosystem, without requiring of the consumer the impossible proof of a black box.<1>p. 471</1>

On the sanction side, the case of the irregular gifts, treated in the chapter on proof, shows the other extreme of the problem. Once the assets are removed or the state of the account is reverted, what is called a rollback, the user comes to depend on old statements, scattered emails and screenshots to prove that a given content was part of his position of enjoyment. In qualified cases, the episode serves as a bridge to open auditability, because the dispute exposes the need for verifiable transparency about criteria for change, rollback and sanction.

Once the assets are removed or the state of the account is reverted, the user comes to depend on old statements, scattered emails, past captures and reconstructed memory to prove that a given content legitimately was part of his position of enjoyment.<1>p. 616</1>
On the one hand, to open auditability, because the dispute exposes the need for verifiable transparency about criteria for change, rollback and sanction.<1>p. 617</1>
What happens when the auditable minimum does not come?

There is a breach of the parameter whenever relevant changes in access, performance, utility, operating rule or sanction fall on enjoyment without preservation of minimum reconstruction trails. When the supplier, faced with a relevant change, does not deliver the auditable minimum compatible with the consumer relationship, the transparency must be treated as inadequate. Depending on the intensity of the case, this inadequacy may work as evidence or direct manifestation of structural abusiveness of the supply regime, so there is no automatism in the passage from one thing to the other. In practical terms, this legitimizes obligations to perform aimed at the preservation and display of records, the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions favorable to the consumer in the face of unjustified refusal to cooperate and the control of the validity or effectiveness of clauses and policies that seek to shield non-verifiable changes.

In terms of remedy, it means that the absence of trails and of verifiability ceases to be an operational detail and becomes part of the unlawful act itself.<1>p. 636</1>

The passage from the parameter to procedure is left to the chapter on proof, which deals with qualified communication, the minimum documentary core, requests for production of documents, expert examination and the redistribution of the burden. It is enough here to record the link. The CDC was not designed for the supplier to turn the harm into an accounting cost, and it already has instruments compatible with production of documents, early production of evidence and specific relief. Bruno Miragem highlights the prevalence of specific performance and the actions for production of documents. Without access to the relevant versions, to the execution records and to the elements that demonstrate the supply performed, the legal discussion runs the risk of being held hostage to the documentary fiction of the base contract, which often says little about the real life of the service<1>p. 646</1>

Specific performance of the obligation prevails precisely to prevent the supplier from turning nonperformance into an advantageous economic calculation, converting harms into losses and damages as an ordinary cost of the business. For this reason, conversion into indemnification should only occur at the consumer's option or when specific relief or the equivalent practical result is impossible <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 898)</2>.<3>p. 646</3>

This design is articulated with preliminary measures aimed at the early production of evidence, notably actions for production of documents, especially in disputes in which the contractual instrument was not delivered to the consumer or in which the actual content of the relationship needs to be reconstructed <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 903)</2>.<3>p. 646</3>
All the mechanisms answer the same requirement: to prevent the supplier's exclusive technical control from turning into a monopoly over the proof of the very unlawful act alleged.<1>p. 663</1>

Auditability alone does not decide the material legitimacy of the change, because demonstrating what changed does not answer whether the change preserved the substance of the acquired enjoyment. This second question belongs to functional value equivalence, the subject of a chapter of its own. The two criteria presuppose each other, since without auditability equivalence is hard to demonstrate and without equivalence auditability runs the risk of becoming a mere capacity to narrate changes. In short, one controls the how of the mutation and the other, the how much and the what, and from this come two tests for the interpreter. The first is whether there was minimum institutional verifiability, with reasoning, timing, effects and reconstruction trails. The second is whether the change preserved sufficient functional equivalence or significantly lowered the practical and symbolic core of the object. The order matters, because first the change is reconstructed and then its legitimacy is measured. When one of the tests fails, the change becomes legally suspect, and when both fail, the hypothesis strongly approaches a supply defect, an abusive practice, a breach of trust or an architecture of structural opacity.

On its own, open auditability does not resolve the whole dispute, because demonstrating what changed and how it changed does not exhaust the question of the material legitimacy of the change.<1>p. 647</1>
One standard controls the how of the mutation; the other, the how much and the what of the mutation.<1>p. 638</1>

First, was there minimum institutional verifiability of the change, with reasoning, timing, effects and reconstruction trails of the supply? Second, did the change preserve sufficient functional equivalence with the legitimately acquired enjoyment, or did it significantly lower the practical and symbolic core of the object?<1>p. 639</1>
First, the change is reconstructed. Then, its material legitimacy is measured. This order matters. Without it, the supplier will always have the advantage of the fog.<1>p. 647</1>

When one of these conditions fails, the legitimacy of the change already becomes legally suspect. When both fail at the same time, the hypothesis strongly approaches a supply defect, an abusive practice, a breach of trust or even an architecture of structural opacity incompatible with the consumer regime.<1>p. 638-639</1>
Isn't auditing the same as opening the trade secret?

The first is the objection of secrecy, according to which requiring auditability would amount to opening the code, handing over the trade secret and leaving the software unprotected. The answer is that the legal order already lives with limited forms of scrutiny that preserve the informational asset, such as judicial secrecy, restricted expert access, delimited functional analysis and institutional control. Denis Borges Barbosa records that judicial secrecy restricts third-party access to sensitive information, such as source code, and prevents its use by the opposing party for purposes foreign to the dispute. The reconciliation between protecting the asset and the need for verification, therefore, is nothing new.
The protection of software does not turn it into a sacred black box.<1>p. 643</1>

This point is important because the business objection usually comes in predictable garb: requiring auditability would amount to requiring the opening of code, the handing over of the trade secret, the exposure of know-how or the unprotection of the software.<1>p. 643</1>
Judicial secrecy, restricted expert access, delimited functional analysis, technically necessary use for certain purposes and institutional control are not demolitions of exclusivity.<1>p. 643</1>

The legal discipline itself provides for judicial secrecy, which restricts third-party access to sensitive information, such as source code, and prevents its use by the opposing party for purposes foreign to the dispute <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1940)</2>.<3>p. 643</3>

The secret also has to be shown in order to be protected. Generically invoking secrecy or technical sensitivity, without delimiting what needs to remain reserved, is not enough, and Barbosa observes that, for there to be judicial control, it is necessary to identify what the secret is, because the broad assertion that it relates to the company's field of activity does not allow such control. The protection remains legitimate, but what interests Consumer Law is not, as a rule, the internal ingenuity of the program, but how a certain operating regime, a certain change or a certain criterion affected enjoyment. The examination falls on the functioning for purposes of control, and not on the parasitic appropriation of the asset. When technical decisions condition permanence in the service on invasive requirements, the need for the platform not to hide behind technical opacity and trade secrets is reinforced.
The company can still protect its secret. What it cannot do is want secrecy over the very impact of the change it imposed on the consumer.<1>p. 644</1>

Generically invoking “secrecy” or “technical sensitivity” without delimiting what actually needs to remain reserved and without admitting any form of institutionally relevant reconstruction is not enough.<1>p. 644</1>
For confidentiality to be legally respected, it needs to be identified and carved out, not treated as a magic fog that dissolves every requirement of accountability.<1>p. 644</1>

For the hypothesis to be submitted to judicial control, “it is necessary to unveil and identify what secret would have been disclosed”, it not being enough to allege, broadly, that it is a secret related to the company's field of activity, because such a sweeping assertion does not allow effective judicial control of the dispute <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392)</2>.<3>p. 644</3>
The legally relevant examination falls on the functioning for purposes of control, not on the parasitic appropriation of the asset.<1>p. 644</1>

When technical decisions and internal policies expand the extraterritoriality of code, conditioning permanence and participation on invasive requirements or on control mechanisms that exceed the perimeter of the contracted object, the claim to practical sovereignty over the consumer and over his material means becomes evident, which reinforces the need for open auditability as a minimum requirement so that the platform does not hide behind technical opacity and trade secrets, and so that governance by architecture is treated as imputable conduct, contestable and subject to proportionality.<1>p. 499</1>

The second is the objection of technical complexity. Without the parameter, the supplier can always claim that it changed for technical reasons, that it informed as best it could, that the impact was small, that the change was provided for in some document and that the consumer simply did not understand or did not like it. With it, it becomes possible to ask what was changed, on what basis, with what effect and with what reconstruction trails. The generic invocation of internal policy, security, service improvement or ecosystem integrity does not work as a self-sufficient justification, and legitimate complexity is not to be confused with obscurity used as a technique of power.
In continuous consumer relationships, complexity does not revoke good faith.<1>p. 647</1>

Without this standard, the supplier can always claim that it changed for technical reasons, that it informed as best it could, that the impact was small, that the change was provided for in some document and that the consumer simply did not understand or did not like it.<1>p. 645</1>

On the other, it prevents the generic invocation of “internal policy”, “security”, “service improvement” or “ecosystem integrity” from working as a self-sufficient justification immune to control, emptying duties of information, loyalty and adequacy in continued performance.<1>p. 473</1>
In governed environments, this is what separates legitimate complexity from obscurity functionalized as a technique of power.<1>p. 728</1>

The third is that the requirement would multiply technical litigation. The opposite occurs, because the parameter has a containment function. With preserved trails, identifiable versions and statable reasons, the endless war of opaque technicalities is avoided, in which each side speaks a different language and the decision ends up handed over to intuitive deference to the more organized party. Expert examinations, production of documents and clarification orders come to fall on knowable objects, and the dispute is delimited.
Open auditability also performs a function of containing litigation.<1>p. 728</1>

When there are preserved trails, identifiable relevant versions, minimally statable reasons for change and basic elements for reconstructing the conflict, the judicial discussion is prevented from turning into an endless war of opaque technicalities, in which each side speaks a different language and the decision ends up handed over to intuitive deference to the more organized party.<1>p. 728</1>

The fourth is that the parameter invents a right or stifles innovation. As to invention, besides the rooting in the duty to inform, there is the support of Karl Larenz, who describes the legal system as open and, to a certain degree, mobile, so that the two operators do not replace the system and allow it to see through controllable criteria what abbreviated formulas tend to erase. As to innovation, the answer is that auditability is a criterion of legitimacy of platform architectures, and not hostility toward them. Platforms may innovate, update, fix, rebalance, migrate and protect their technical assets. What they cannot do is do so under a regime of institutional irreconstructibility.

Larenz describes the system as an “‘open’ system and, to a certain degree, a ‘mobile’ one”, always incomplete and continually put into question, whose function is to make clear the “intrinsic rationality”, the guiding values and the principles of Law <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 241)</2>.<3>p. 481</3>

Open auditability and functional value equivalence occupy this place: they do not replace the system; they allow it to see, through controllable criteria, what abbreviated formulas tend to erase.<1>p. 481</1>

For this reason, open auditability must be understood as a criterion of legitimacy of platform architectures, and not as abstract hostility toward them. Platforms may innovate, update, fix, rebalance, migrate and protect their technical assets. What they cannot do is do so under a regime of institutional irreconstructibility, as if the very complexity of the system authorized them to decide alone what matters, what was changed and what may or may not be known by those who enjoy the service and by those who control it legally.<1>p. 647</1>
What does open auditability not reach?

The name calls for a careful reading. Open auditability does not require total transparency, unrestricted opening of the infrastructure, exposure of source code, the full architecture of the system or sensitive trade secrets, nor complete opening of proprietary models and metrics. Nor does it require absolute explainability or technical omniscience of the judge, and the platform remains the holder of its intangible assets and of its internal architecture. Whoever frames the claim as a full search of the system asks for what the parameter does not give.

The name needs to be read carefully so as not to produce misunderstanding. It is not a matter of requiring the opening of code, a total search of the infrastructure, full publicity of internal systems or theatrical laboratory transparency.<1>p. 636</1>

We are not faced with a requirement of total transparency, nor with unrestricted opening of the technical infrastructure, nor with an obligation to expose source code, the full architecture of the system or sensitive trade secrets.<1>p. 640</1>
Its focus is not to produce full transparency of the technical-organizational environment nor to impose complete opening of models, source code, proprietary metrics or trade secrets.<1>p. 472</1>
The parameter is calibrated precisely to make control possible without requiring technical omniscience of the judge or disorganizing the economic functioning of the ecosystem.<1>p. 728</1>

The platform remains the holder of its intangible assets and of its internal architecture, but can no longer invoke them to prevent, completely, the institutional reconstruction of events that affect the consumer's enjoyment in a legally relevant way.<1>p. 729</1>

As to the changes reached, the parameter leaves out the microscopic adjustment, the cosmetic change and the irrelevant fluctuation, and does not turn each update into litigation. Not every change is unlawful, and not every improvement becomes a problem, because updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility. As to the effects, the lack of auditability makes the change legally suspect, and the inadequacy of transparency only reaches structural abusiveness depending on the intensity of the case. What the parameter delivers is a basis for reconstruction, without dispensing with the material examination of equivalence.
This problem does not turn every improvement into an unlawful act. Updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem.<1>p. 470</1>
The section, thus, does not turn every change into an unlawful act. It merely refuses that the change become an automatic alibi for irresponsibility.<1>p. 639</1>

What remains, after these cuts, is a minimum that the supplier cannot refuse without consequence. Business secrecy, economic exclusivity and the complexity of the service cease to operate as absolute vetoes and become elements to be reconciled with duties of minimum verifiability. Opacity ceases to be a zone naturally immune to protection and becomes a legal problem treatable by preservation orders, delimited production of documents, restricted expert examination and verifiable reasoning. The mutability of the service remains possible, without standing above legal control, and private governance ceases to approach a practical sovereignty.
Technical opacity, by itself, does not work as a free zone of liability.<1>p. 481</1>

Business secrecy, economic exclusivity and the complexity of the service cease to operate as absolute vetoes on control and become elements to be reconciled with duties of minimum verifiability.<1>p. 728-729</1>

Structural opacity thus ceases to be a zone naturally immune to protection and becomes a legal problem treatable by preservation orders, delimited production of documents, restricted expert examination, verifiable reasoning and other instruments compatible with the procedural and administrative rationality of the protective system.<1>p. 729</1>
